You'd have to think the world very stupid if they didn't believe that the profits you'd get from my death were obvious, powerful reasons for you to want it.'
Strong and fast'ned villain! / Would he deny his letter?—I never got him.
Hardened, determined villain! Would he deny his own letter? He's no son of mine.

Hark, the duke's trumpets! I know not why he comes.— / All ports I'll bar; the villain shall not scape; / The duke must grant me that: besides, his picture / I will send far and near, that all the kingdom / May have due note of him; and of my land, / Loyal and natural boy, I'll work the means / To make thee capable.

Listen, the Duke's trumpets! I don't know why he's coming. I'll block all the ports. The villain won't escape. The Duke must allow me that. Besides, I'll send his picture far and wide so the whole kingdom will know him. And as for my land, my loyal and natural son, I'll find a way to make you able to inherit it.
How now, my noble friend! since I came hither,— / Which I can call but now,—I have heard strange news.
Well, my noble friend! Since I arrived, which was only just now, I've heard strange news.
If it be true, all vengeance comes too short / Which can pursue the offender. How dost, my lord?
If it's true, no punishment is enough for the offender. How are you, my lord?
O madam, my old heart is crack'd,—it's crack'd!
Oh, madam, my old heart is broken, it's broken!
What, did my father's godson seek your life? / He whom my father nam'd? your Edgar?
What, did my father's godson try to kill you? The one my father named? Your Edgar?
O lady, lady, shame would have it hid!
Oh, lady, lady, I'd hide it out of shame!
Was he not companion with the riotous knights / That tend upon my father?
Wasn't he friends with the rowdy knights who serve my father?
I know not, madam:— / It is too bad, too bad.
I don't know, madam. It's too bad, too bad.
Yes, madam, he was of that consort.
Yes, madam, he was one of that gang.

No marvel then though he were ill affected: / 'Tis they have put him on the old man's death, / To have the expense and waste of his revenues. / I have this present evening from my sister / Been well inform'd of them; and with such cautions / That if they come to sojourn at my house, / I'll not be there.

No wonder he went bad, then. It's they who have put him up to killing the old man, so they can spend and waste his income. This very evening my sister told me all about them, with such warnings that if they come to stay at my house, I won't be there.
Nor I, assure thee, Regan.— / Edmund, I hear that you have shown your father / A childlike office.
Nor I, I promise you, Regan. Edmund, I hear you have done your father a true son's service.
He did bewray his practice; and receiv'd / This hurt you see, striving to apprehend him.
He exposed Edgar's plot, and got this wound you see trying to arrest him.

If he be taken, he shall never more / Be fear'd of doing harm: make your own purpose, / How in my strength you please.—For you, Edmund, / Whose virtue and obedience doth this instant / So much commend itself, you shall be ours: / Natures of such deep trust we shall much need; / You we first seize on.

If he's caught, he'll never be feared again. Make your plans, using my power however you like. As for you, Edmund, whose goodness and obedience show so well right now, you'll serve me. I'll need men I can trust so deeply. You're the first I take.
I shall serve you, sir, / Truly, however else.
I'll serve you faithfully, sir, whatever else I do.
For him I thank your grace.
I thank your grace for him.
You know not why we came to visit you,—
You don't know why we've come to visit you...

Thus out of season, threading dark-ey'd night: / Occasions, noble Gloster, of some poise, / Wherein we must have use of your advice:— / Our father he hath writ, so hath our sister, / Of differences, which I best thought it fit / To answer from our home; the several messengers / From hence attend despatch. Our good old friend, / Lay comforts to your bosom; and bestow / Your needful counsel to our business, / Which craves the instant use.

...so unexpectedly, travelling through the dark night. There are matters of some weight, noble Gloster, on which we need your advice. Our father has written, and so has our sister, about their quarrels, and I thought it best to answer away from our home. The messengers are waiting here to be sent back. Our good old friend, comfort yourself, and give us the advice our business needs, as it needs it right away.
I serve you, madam: / Your graces are right welcome.
I'm at your service, madam. Your graces are very welcome.
Good dawning to thee, friend: art of this house?
Good morning to you, friend. Do you belong to this house?
Where may we set our horses?
Where can we put our horses?
Pr'ythee, if thou lov'st me, tell me.
Please, if you love me, tell me.
Why then, I care not for thee.
Well then, I don't care about you.
If I had thee in Lipsbury pinfold, I would make thee care for me.
If I had you between my teeth, I'd make you care about me.
Why dost thou use me thus? I know thee not.
Why are you treating me like this? I don't know you.
What dost thou know me for?
What do you know me as?

A knave; a rascal; an eater of broken meats; a base, proud, / shallow, beggarly, three-suited, hundred-pound, filthy, / worsted-stocking knave; a lily-livered, action-taking, whoreson, / glass-gazing, superserviceable, finical rogue; / one-trunk-inheriting slave; one that wouldst be a bawd in way of / good service, and art nothing but the composition of a / knave, beggar, coward, pander, and the son and heir of a mongrel / bitch: one whom I will beat into clamorous whining, if thou / denyest the least syllable of thy addition.

A rogue, a rascal, an eater of leftover scraps. A low, proud, shallow, beggarly servant with three suits and a hundred-pound income, a filthy rogue in cheap wool stockings. A lily-livered, cowardly, lawsuit-running son of a whore, a mirror-gazing, over-eager, fussy rogue, a slave whose whole inheritance fits in one trunk. Someone who'd be a pimp if it pleased his master, and who is nothing but a mixture of rogue, beggar, coward and pimp, and the son and heir of a mongrel bitch. I'll beat you till you whine and howl if you deny the smallest syllable of these titles.
Why, what a monstrous fellow art thou, thus to rail on one that's / neither known of thee nor knows thee?
What a monstrous fellow you are, to insult someone you don't know and who doesn't know you!

What a brazen-faced varlet art thou, to deny thou knowest me! Is / it two days ago since I beat thee and tripped up thy heels before / the king? Draw, you rogue: for, though it be night, yet the moon / shines; I'll make a sop o' the moonshine of you: draw, you / whoreson cullionly barbermonger, draw! / [Drawing his sword.]

What a shameless rascal you are to deny you know me! Is it two days since I tripped you up and beat you in front of the King? Draw, you rogue. Although it's night, the moon is shining. I'll soak you full of moonshine like bread in soup. Draw, you son-of-a-whore, contemptible dandy, draw! [He draws his sword.]
Away! I have nothing to do with thee.
Get away! I have nothing to do with you.

Draw, you rascal: you come with letters against the king; and / take vanity the puppet's part against the royalty of her father: / draw, you rogue, or I'll so carbonado your shanks:— / draw, you rascal; come your ways!

Draw, you rascal. You come with letters against the King, and take the side of that puppet Vanity against the royalty of her father. Draw, you rogue, or I'll slice your legs like meat for grilling. Draw, you rascal. Come on!
Strike, you slave; stand, rogue, stand; you neat slave, strike!
Fight, you slave! Stand still, rogue, stand still! You dressed-up slave, fight!
With you, goodman boy, an you please: come, I'll flesh you; come / on, young master.
I'll fight you, young sir, if you like. Come on, I'll give you your first taste of blood. Come on, young master.
Weapons! arms! What's the matter here?
Weapons! Swords! What's going on here?
Keep peace, upon your lives; / He dies that strikes again. What is the matter?
Keep the peace, on your lives! The next man who strikes dies. What's the matter?
The messengers from our sister and the king.
The messengers from our sister and the King.
I am scarce in breath, my lord.
I'm out of breath, my lord.
No marvel, you have so bestirr'd your valour. You cowardly / rascal, nature disclaims in thee; a tailor made thee.
No wonder, you've worked your courage so hard. You cowardly rascal, nature disowns you. A tailor made you.
Thou art a strange fellow: a tailor make a man?
You're a strange fellow. A tailor make a man?
Ay, a tailor, sir: a stonecutter or a painter could not have / made him so ill, though he had been but two hours at the trade.
Yes, a tailor, sir. A sculptor or a painter couldn't have made him so badly, even after only two hours of training.
Speak yet, how grew your quarrel?
Go on, tell me how your quarrel started.
This ancient ruffian, sir, whose life I have spared at suit of / his grey / beard,—
This old ruffian, sir, whose life I spared because of his grey beard...

Thou whoreson zed! thou unnecessary letter!—My lord, if you'll / give me leave, I will tread this unbolted villain into mortar and / daub the walls of a jakes with him.—Spare my grey beard, you / wagtail?
You son-of-a-whore Z! You useless letter! My lord, if you'll let me, I'll stamp this lumpy villain into mortar and plaster the walls of a toilet with him. Spare my grey beard, you bobbing wagtail?
Peace, sirrah! / You beastly knave, know you no reverence?
Quiet, fellow! You beastly rogue, have you no respect?
Yes, sir; but anger hath a privilege.
Yes, sir, but anger has its privileges.

That such a slave as this should wear a sword, / Who wears no honesty. Such smiling rogues as these, / Like rats, oft bite the holy cords a-twain / Which are too intrinse t' unloose; smooth every passion / That in the natures of their lords rebel; / Bring oil to fire, snow to their colder moods; / Renege, affirm, and turn their halcyon beaks / With every gale and vary of their masters, / Knowing naught, like dogs, but following.— / A plague upon your epileptic visage! / Smile you my speeches, as I were a fool? / Goose, an I had you upon Sarum plain, / I'd drive ye cackling home to Camelot.

That a slave like this should wear a sword when he has no honesty. Smiling rogues like him, like rats, often bite through the holy bonds that are too tight to untie. They flatter every passion that rebels in their masters' natures, bring oil to their fire and snow to their colder moods. They deny, agree and turn their beaks like a weathervane bird with every change in their masters' moods, knowing nothing, like dogs, except how to follow. A plague on your twitching face! Are you smirking at my speeches as if I were a fool? You goose, if I had you on Salisbury Plain, I'd chase you cackling all the way home to Camelot.
What, art thou mad, old fellow?
What, are you mad, old fellow?
How fell you out? / Say that.
How did you fall out? Tell us that.
No contraries hold more antipathy / Than I and such a knave.
No two opposites hate each other more than I and a rogue like this.
Why dost thou call him knave? What is his fault?
Why do you call him a rogue? What has he done wrong?
No more perchance does mine, or his, or hers.
Perhaps you don't like mine either, or his, or hers.
Sir, 'tis my occupation to be plain: / I have seen better faces in my time / Than stands on any shoulder that I see / Before me at this instant.
Sir, it's my job to be blunt. I've seen better faces in my time than any on the shoulders I see in front of me right now.

This is some fellow / Who, having been prais'd for bluntness, doth affect / A saucy roughness, and constrains the garb / Quite from his nature: he cannot flatter, he,— / An honest mind and plain,—he must speak truth! / An they will take it, so; if not, he's plain. / These kind of knaves I know which in this plainness / Harbour more craft and more corrupter ends / Than twenty silly-ducking observants / That stretch their duties nicely.

This is some fellow who, having been praised for his bluntness, puts on a cheeky roughness and twists his manner away from his true nature. He can't flatter, not he! An honest, plain mind, he must speak the truth! If they'll take it, fine. If not, he's just plain. I know rogues like this, who hide more cunning and more corrupt aims in their plainness than twenty silly, bowing servants who carry out their duties with fussy care.
Sir, in good faith, in sincere verity, / Under the allowance of your great aspect, / Whose influence, like the wreath of radiant fire / On flickering Phoebus' front,—
Sir, in good faith and sincere truth, with the permission of your great presence, whose influence, like the ring of shining fire on the bright sun's forehead...
What do you mean by this?

To go out of my dialect, which you discommend so much. I know, / sir, I am no flatterer: he that beguiled you in a plain accent / was a plain knave; which, for my part, I will not be, though I / should win your displeasure to entreat me to't.

To get away from my usual way of speaking, which you dislike so much. I know, sir, I'm no flatterer. The man who tricked you with plain speaking was a plain rogue, which I won't be, even if I could get you to stop being displeased and beg me to be one.
What was the offence you gave him?

I never gave him any: / It pleas'd the king his master very late / To strike at me, upon his misconstruction; / When he, compact, and flattering his displeasure, / Tripp'd me behind; being down, insulted, rail'd / And put upon him such a deal of man, / That worthied him, got praises of the king / For him attempting who was self-subdu'd; / And, in the fleshment of this dread exploit, / Drew on me here again.

I never did. The King his master recently decided to hit me because he misunderstood me. Then this man, siding with him and flattering his anger, tripped me from behind. When I was down, he insulted me, abused me and made himself out such a hero that he won praise from the King for attacking a man who didn't fight back. Thrilled by this terrible exploit, he drew his sword on me again here.
None of these rogues and cowards / But Ajax is their fool.
Rogues and cowards like these all make Ajax look like a fool next to them.
Fetch forth the stocks!— / You stubborn ancient knave, you reverent braggart, / We'll teach you,—
Bring out the stocks! You stubborn old rogue, you respected boaster, we'll teach you...

Sir, I am too old to learn: / Call not your stocks for me: I serve the king; / On whose employment I was sent to you: / You shall do small respect, show too bold malice / Against the grace and person of my master, / Stocking his messenger.

Sir, I'm too old to learn. Don't send for the stocks for me. I serve the King, who sent me on business to you. You'll show little respect and too bold a malice against the dignity and person of my master if you put his messenger in the stocks.
Fetch forth the stocks!—As I have life and honour, / there shall he sit till noon.
Bring out the stocks! As I live and value my honour, he'll sit there till noon.
Till noon! Till night, my lord; and all night too!
Till noon! Till night, my lord, and all night too!
Why, madam, if I were your father's dog, / You should not use me so.
Why, madam, if I were your father's dog, you shouldn't treat me like this.
Sir, being his knave, I will.
Sir, since you're his servant, I will.
This is a fellow of the self-same colour / Our sister speaks of.—Come, bring away the stocks!
This is a fellow of exactly the same type our sister writes about. Come, bring the stocks!

Let me beseech your grace not to do so: / His fault is much, and the good king his master / Will check him for't: your purpos'd low correction / Is such as basest and contemned'st wretches / For pilferings and most common trespasses, / Are punish'd with: the king must take it ill / That he, so slightly valu'd in his messenger, / Should have him thus restrain'd.

Let me beg your grace not to do this. His fault is great, and his good master the King will punish him for it. The low punishment you intend is the kind used for the lowest, most despised wretches for petty theft and the commonest crimes. The King must take it badly that he is so little respected that his messenger is treated like this.
My sister may receive it much more worse, / To have her gentleman abus'd, assaulted, / For following her affairs.—Put in his legs.—
My sister may take it much worse that her gentleman was abused and attacked for carrying out her business. Put his legs in.
Come, my good lord, let's go.
I am sorry for thee, friend; 'tis the duke's pleasure, / Whose disposition, all the world well knows, / Will not be rubb'd nor stopp'd; I'll entreat for thee.
I'm sorry for you, friend. It's the Duke's wish, and everyone knows his temper won't be blocked or stopped. I'll plead for you.
Pray do not, sir: I have watch'd, and travell'd hard; / Some time I shall sleep out, the rest I'll whistle. / A good man's fortune may grow out at heels: / Give you good morrow!
Please don't, sir. I've gone without sleep and travelled hard. I'll spend some of the time sleeping and the rest whistling. Even a good man's luck can wear out at the heels. Good morning to you!
The duke's to blame in this: 'twill be ill taken.
The Duke is to blame for this. It will go down badly.

Good king, that must approve the common saw,— / Thou out of heaven's benediction com'st / To the warm sun! / Approach, thou beacon to this under globe, / That by thy comfortable beams I may / Peruse this letter.—Nothing almost sees miracles / But misery:—I know 'tis from Cordelia, / Who hath most fortunately been inform'd / Of my obscured course; and shall find time / From this enormous state,—seeking to give / Losses their remedies,—All weary and o'erwatch'd, / Take vantage, heavy eyes, not to behold / This shameful lodging. / Fortune, good night: smile once more, turn thy wheel!

Good King, you're proving the old saying true: you are going from heaven's blessing out into the hot sun! Come up, you sun, beacon to this world below, so that by your comforting rays I can read this letter. Almost nobody sees miracles except the miserable. I know it's from Cordelia, who has very luckily been told of my disguise, and who will find a chance to fix this monstrous situation and put right what has gone wrong. Weary and exhausted, heavy eyes, take the chance not to look at this shameful lodging. Fortune, good night. Smile once more and turn your wheel!

I heard myself proclaim'd; / And by the happy hollow of a tree / Escap'd the hunt. No port is free; no place / That guard and most unusual vigilance / Does not attend my taking. While I may scape, / I will preserve myself: and am bethought / To take the basest and most poorest shape / That ever penury, in contempt of man, / Brought near to beast: my face I'll grime with filth; / Blanket my loins; elf all my hair in knots; / And with presented nakedness outface / The winds and persecutions of the sky. / The country gives me proof and precedent / Of Bedlam beggars, who, with roaring voices, / Strike in their numb'd and mortified bare arms / Pins, wooden pricks, nails, sprigs of rosemary; / And with this horrible object, from low farms, / Poor pelting villages, sheep-cotes, and mills, / Sometime with lunatic bans, sometime with prayers, / Enforce their charity.—Poor Turlygod! poor Tom! / That's something yet:—Edgar I nothing am.

I heard myself declared an outlaw, and escaped the hunt by hiding in a lucky hollow tree. No port is open, and there's no place without guards and unusually close watch waiting to catch me. While I can escape, I'll save myself. I've decided to take on the lowest and poorest appearance that poverty ever brought close to an animal in contempt of man. I'll smear my face with filth, wear only a blanket round my waist, tangle all my hair into knots, and with my body bare I'll face the winds and storms of the sky. The countryside gives me the example of Bedlam beggars, madmen who with roaring voices stick pins, wooden skewers, nails and sprigs of rosemary into their numb, deadened bare arms, and with this horrible sight, sometimes with mad curses, sometimes with prayers, force charity out of poor farms, wretched villages, sheepfolds and mills. Poor Turlygod! Poor Tom! That's something at least. As Edgar, I am nothing.
'Tis strange that they should so depart from home, / And not send back my messenger.
It's strange that they should leave home like that and not send my messenger back.
As I learn'd, / The night before there was no purpose in them / Of this remove.
As I heard it, the night before they had no plan to move.
Ha! / Mak'st thou this shame thy pastime?
Ha! Are you doing this shameful thing for fun?

Ha, ha! he wears cruel garters. Horses are tied by the / head; dogs and bears by the neck, monkeys by the loins, and / men by the legs: when a man is over-lusty at legs, then he / wears wooden nether-stocks.
Ha, ha! He's wearing cruel garters. Horses are tied by the head, dogs and bears by the neck, monkeys by the waist and men by the legs. When a man is too ready to run, he wears wooden stockings.
What's he that hath so much thy place mistook / To set thee here?
Who misjudged your rank so much as to put you here?
It is both he and she, / Your son and daughter.
It was both he and she: your son-in-law and your daughter.

They durst not do't. / They would not, could not do't; 'tis worse than murder, / To do upon respect such violent outrage: / Resolve me, with all modest haste, which way / Thou mightst deserve or they impose this usage, / Coming from us.

They wouldn't dare do it. They wouldn't, couldn't do it. It's worse than murder to do such violent outrage to the respect owed to me. Tell me, as quickly as you decently can, how you could deserve or they could impose this treatment, when you came from me.

My lord, when at their home / I did commend your highness' letters to them, / Ere I was risen from the place that show'd / My duty kneeling, came there a reeking post, / Stew'd in his haste, half breathless, panting forth / From Goneril his mistress salutations; / Deliver'd letters, spite of intermission, / Which presently they read: on whose contents, / They summon'd up their meiny, straight took horse; / Commanded me to follow and attend / The leisure of their answer; gave me cold looks: / And meeting here the other messenger, / Whose welcome I perceiv'd had poison'd mine,— / Being the very fellow which of late / Display'd so saucily against your highness,— / Having more man than wit about me, drew: / He rais'd the house with loud and coward cries. / Your son and daughter found this trespass worth / The shame which here it suffers.

My lord, when I delivered your highness's letters to them at their home, before I'd even got up from kneeling to show my duty, a sweating messenger arrived, steaming from his hurry, half out of breath, gasping out greetings from his mistress Goneril. He handed over letters, interrupting me, which they read at once. Because of what they said, they called their servants together and got straight on their horses. They ordered me to follow and wait until they had time to answer, and gave me cold looks. Then, meeting the other messenger here, whose welcome I could see had poisoned mine, and who was the very fellow who recently behaved so insolently to your highness, I had more courage than sense and drew my sword. He woke the house with loud, cowardly screams. Your son-in-law and daughter thought this offence deserved the shame it's suffering here.

Winter's not gone yet, if the wild geese fly that way. / Fathers that wear rags / Do make their children blind; / But fathers that bear bags / Shall see their children kind. / Fortune, that arrant whore, / Ne'er turns the key to th' poor. / But for all this, thou shalt have as many dolours for thy / daughters as thou canst tell in a year.

Winter isn't over yet if the wild geese are flying that way. Fathers who wear rags make their children blind, but fathers who carry money bags will see their children kind. Fortune, that total whore, never opens the door to the poor. But for all this, you'll have as many sorrows from your daughters as you can count in a year.
O, how this mother swells up toward my heart! / Hysterica passio,—down, thou climbing sorrow, / Thy element's below!—Where is this daughter?
Oh, how this hysteria swells up towards my heart! Rising sickness, get down, you climbing sorrow, your place is lower down! Where is this daughter?
With the earl, sir, here within.
Made you no more offence but what you speak of?
Did you do nothing more wrong than what you've told us?
None. / How chance the king comes with so small a number?
Nothing. How is it the King comes with so few followers?
An thou hadst been set i' the stocks for that question, / thou hadst well deserved it.
If you'd been put in the stocks for asking that, you'd have deserved it.

We'll set thee to school to an ant, to teach thee there's no / labouring in the winter. All that follow their noses are led by / their eyes but blind men; and there's not a nose among twenty / but can smell him that's stinking. Let go thy hold when a great / wheel runs down a hill, lest it break thy neck with following / it; but the great one that goes up the hill, let him draw thee / after. / When a wise man gives thee better counsel, give me mine again: I / would have none but knaves follow it, since a fool gives it. / That sir which serves and seeks for gain, / And follows but for form, / Will pack when it begins to rain, / And leave thee in the storm. / But I will tarry; the fool will stay, / And let the wise man fly: / The knave turns fool that runs away; / The fool no knave, perdy.

We'll send you to school with an ant, to teach you there's no work in winter. Everyone who follows his nose is led by his eyes, except blind men, and there isn't one nose in twenty that can't smell a man who stinks of bad luck. Let go when a great wheel is running downhill, in case it breaks your neck as you follow it. But when a great man is going up the hill, let him pull you up after him. When a wise man gives you better advice, give me mine back. I'd want only rogues to follow it, since a fool gives it. The man who serves for profit and follows only for show will pack up when it starts to rain and leave you in the storm. But I will wait, the Fool will stay, and let the wise man run away. The rogue who runs away turns out the fool; the fool, by God, is no rogue.
Where did you learn this, Fool?
Deny to speak with me? They are sick? they are weary? / They have travell'd all the night? Mere fetches; / The images of revolt and flying off. / Fetch me a better answer.
Refuse to speak to me? They're ill? They're tired? They've travelled all night? Just excuses, signs of rebellion and desertion. Get me a better answer.
My dear lord, / You know the fiery quality of the duke; / How unremovable and fix'd he is / In his own course.
My dear lord, you know how fiery the Duke is, how immovable and fixed he is in his own way.
Vengeance! plague! death! confusion!— / Fiery? What quality? why, Gloster, Gloster, / I'd speak with the Duke of Cornwall and his wife.
Vengeance! Plague! Death! Destruction! Fiery? What kind of temper? Why, Gloster, Gloster, I want to speak to the Duke of Cornwall and his wife.
Well, my good lord, I have inform'd them so.
Well, my good lord, I've told them so.
Inform'd them! Dost thou understand me, man?
Told them! Do you understand me, man?

The King would speak with Cornwall; the dear father / Would with his daughter speak, commands her service: / Are they inform'd of this?—My breath and blood!— / Fiery? the fiery duke?—Tell the hot duke that— / No, but not yet: may be he is not well: / Infirmity doth still neglect all office / Whereto our health is bound: we are not ourselves / When nature, being oppress'd, commands the mind / To suffer with the body: I'll forbear; / And am fallen out with my more headier will, / To take the indispos'd and sickly fit / For the sound man.—Death on my state! Wherefore

The King wants to speak with Cornwall. The dear father wants to speak with his daughter, and commands her service. Have they been told this? My breath and blood! Fiery? The fiery Duke? Tell the hot Duke that... No, not yet. Maybe he isn't well. Illness always makes us neglect the duties we are bound to when healthy. We aren't ourselves when nature, overpowered, forces the mind to suffer along with the body. I'll be patient. I'm angry with my own hastier impulse for taking a sick man's fit as the act of a healthy one. Damn my royal state! Why...

Should he sit here? This act persuades me / That this remotion of the duke and her / Is practice only. Give me my servant forth. / Go tell the duke and's wife I'd speak with them, / Now, presently: bid them come forth and hear me, / Or at their chamber door I'll beat the drum / Till it cry 'Sleep to death.'

[Looking at Kent] ...should he sit here? This act convinces me that this moving away of the Duke and her is only a trick. Release my servant. Go and tell the Duke and his wife I want to speak to them, now, at once. Tell them to come out and hear me, or I'll beat the drum at their bedroom door until it kills their sleep.
I would have all well betwixt you.
I wish all were well between you.
O me, my heart, my rising heart!—but down!
Oh, my heart, my rising heart! But get down!

Cry to it, nuncle, as the cockney did to the eels when she / put 'em i' the paste alive; she knapped 'em o' the coxcombs with / a stick and cried 'Down, wantons, down!' 'Twas her brother that, / in pure kindness to his horse, buttered his hay.

Shout at it, uncle, as the silly cook did to the eels when she put them in the pie alive. She whacked them on the head with a stick and shouted 'Down, you naughty things, down!' It was her brother who, out of pure kindness to his horse, buttered its hay.
I am glad to see your highness.
I'm glad to see your highness.

Regan, I think you are; I know what reason / I have to think so: if thou shouldst not be glad, / I would divorce me from thy mother's tomb, / Sepulchring an adultress.—[To Kent] O, are you free? / Some other time for that.—Beloved Regan, / Thy sister's naught: O Regan, she hath tied / Sharp-tooth'd unkindness, like a vulture, here,—

Regan, I think you are. I know why I have reason to think so. If you weren't glad, I'd divorce myself from your mother's tomb, because it would hold an adulteress. [To Kent] Oh, are you free? We'll talk about that another time. Beloved Regan, your sister is wicked. Oh Regan, she has tied sharp-toothed unkindness here, like a vulture... [He points to his heart.]
I can scarce speak to thee; thou'lt not believe / With how deprav'd a quality—O Regan!
I can hardly speak to you. You won't believe how depraved a way... Oh Regan!
I pray you, sir, take patience: I have hope / You less know how to value her desert / Than she to scant her duty.
Please, sir, be patient. I think it's more likely that you don't know how to value her worth than that she would fall short in her duty.

I cannot think my sister in the least / Would fail her obligation: if, sir, perchance / She have restrain'd the riots of your followers, / 'Tis on such ground, and to such wholesome end, / As clears her from all blame.

I can't believe my sister would fail in her obligation in the slightest. If, sir, she has perhaps restrained the riots of your followers, it was for such good reasons and such healthy ends that she can't be blamed at all.

O, sir, you are old; / Nature in you stands on the very verge / Of her confine: you should be rul'd and led / By some discretion, that discerns your state / Better than you yourself. Therefore, I pray you, / That to our sister you do make return; / Say you have wrong'd her, sir.

Oh, sir, you are old. Your life is at the very edge of its limit. You should be ruled and guided by someone sensible who understands your condition better than you do yourself. So please go back to our sister. Tell her you've wronged her, sir.

Ask her forgiveness? / Do you but mark how this becomes the house: / 'Dear daughter, I confess that I am old; / [Kneeling.] / Age is unnecessary: on my knees I beg / That you'll vouchsafe me raiment, bed, and food.'

Ask her forgiveness? Just look how well this suits the royal family: [kneeling] 'Dear daughter, I confess that I am old. Old people are useless. On my knees I beg you to grant me clothes, a bed and food.'
Good sir, no more! These are unsightly tricks: / Return you to my sister.
Good sir, no more of this! These are ugly tricks. Go back to my sister.

[Rising.] Never, Regan: / She hath abated me of half my train; / Look'd black upon me; struck me with her tongue, / Most serpent-like, upon the very heart:— / All the stor'd vengeances of heaven fall / On her ingrateful top! Strike her young bones, / You taking airs, with lameness!

[Rising] Never, Regan. She has cut my followers by half, looked darkly at me, and stung me with her tongue, like a snake, right in the heart. May all the stored-up vengeance of heaven fall on her ungrateful head! Strike her unborn children's bones with lameness, you infectious airs!
You nimble lightnings, dart your blinding flames / Into her scornful eyes! Infect her beauty, / You fen-suck'd fogs, drawn by the powerful sun, / To fall and blast her pride!
You quick lightning, dart your blinding flames into her scornful eyes! Infect her beauty, you fogs sucked up from the marshes by the powerful sun, fall and wither her pride!
O the blest gods! / So will you wish on me when the rash mood is on.
Oh, blessed gods! You'll wish the same on me when your rash mood takes you.

No, Regan, thou shalt never have my curse: / Thy tender-hefted nature shall not give / Thee o'er to harshness: her eyes are fierce; but thine / Do comfort, and not burn. 'Tis not in thee / To grudge my pleasures, to cut off my train, / To bandy hasty words, to scant my sizes, / And, in conclusion, to oppose the bolt / Against my coming in: thou better know'st / The offices of nature, bond of childhood, / Effects of courtesy, dues of gratitude; / Thy half o' the kingdom hast thou not forgot, / Wherein I thee endow'd.

No, Regan, you will never have my curse. Your gentle nature will never let you be harsh. Her eyes are fierce, but yours comfort and don't burn. It's not in you to resent my pleasures, cut down my followers, trade hasty words, reduce my allowance, and, finally, bolt the door against my coming in. You know better the duties of nature, the bonds of a child, the obligations of courtesy and the debts of gratitude. You haven't forgotten the half of the kingdom I gave you.
Good sir, get to the point.
Who put my man i' the stocks?
Who put my man in the stocks?
I know't—my sister's: this approves her letter, / That she would soon be here.
I know it: my sister's. This confirms her letter saying she'd be here soon.
This is a slave, whose easy-borrowed pride / Dwells in the fickle grace of her he follows.— / Out, varlet, from my sight!
This is a slave whose cheaply borrowed pride depends on the fickle favour of the woman he serves. Get out of my sight, you rascal!
Who stock'd my servant? Regan, I have good hope / Thou didst not know on't.—Who comes here? O heavens!
Who put my servant in the stocks? Regan, I hope you didn't know about it. Who's coming? Oh heavens!

If you do love old men, if your sweet sway / Allow obedience, if yourselves are old, / Make it your cause; send down, and take my part!— / [To Goneril.] Art not asham'd to look upon this beard?— / O Regan, wilt thou take her by the hand?

If you love old men, if your gentle rule approves of obedience, if you are old yourselves, make my cause yours. Send down your power and take my side! [To Goneril] Aren't you ashamed to look at this beard? Oh Regan, will you take her by the hand?
Why not by the hand, sir? How have I offended? / All's not offence that indiscretion finds / And dotage terms so.
Why not by the hand, sir? How have I offended? Not everything is an offence just because poor judgement finds it so and senility calls it so.
O sides, you are too tough! / Will you yet hold?—How came my man i' the stocks?
Oh, my ribs, you're too tough! Will you still hold my heart in? How did my man come to be in the stocks?
I set him there, sir: but his own disorders / Deserv'd much less advancement.
I put him there, sir. But his own bad behaviour deserved much less honour than that.

I pray you, father, being weak, seem so. / If, till the expiration of your month, / You will return and sojourn with my sister, / Dismissing half your train, come then to me: / I am now from home, and out of that provision / Which shall be needful for your entertainment.

Please, father, since you are weak, behave like it. If you go back and stay with my sister until the end of your month, dismissing half your followers, then come to me. I'm away from home now and don't have the supplies needed to look after you.

Return to her, and fifty men dismiss'd? / No, rather I abjure all roofs, and choose / To wage against the enmity o' the air; / To be a comrade with the wolf and owl,— / Necessity's sharp pinch!—Return with her? / Why, the hot-blooded France, that dowerless took / Our youngest born, I could as well be brought / To knee his throne, and, squire-like, pension beg / To keep base life afoot.—Return with her? / Persuade me rather to be slave and sumpter / To this detested groom. / [Pointing to Oswald.]

Go back to her, with fifty men dismissed? No, I'd rather give up all roofs and choose to fight against the hostile weather, and be the companion of the wolf and the owl. Need's sharp pinch! Go back with her? Why, I could just as easily be brought to kneel at the throne of that hot-blooded King of France, who took my youngest without a dowry, and beg like a servant for an allowance to keep my miserable life going. Go back with her? Rather persuade me to be a slave and a packhorse to this hateful servant. [He points at Oswald.]

I pr'ythee, daughter, do not make me mad: / I will not trouble thee, my child; farewell: / We'll no more meet, no more see one another:— / But yet thou art my flesh, my blood, my daughter; / Or rather a disease that's in my flesh, / Which I must needs call mine: thou art a boil, / A plague sore, an embossed carbuncle / In my corrupted blood. But I'll not chide thee; / Let shame come when it will, I do not call it: / I do not bid the thunder-bearer shoot / Nor tell tales of thee to high-judging Jove: / Mend when thou canst; be better at thy leisure: / I can be patient; I can stay with Regan, / I and my hundred knights.

Please, daughter, don't drive me mad. I won't trouble you, my child. Goodbye. We'll never meet again, never see each other again. But you are still my flesh, my blood, my daughter. Or rather a disease in my flesh that I have to call mine. You are a boil, a plague sore, a swollen tumour in my diseased blood. But I won't scold you. Let shame come when it will, I won't call for it. I won't ask Jupiter, the thunder-bearer, to strike you, or tell tales about you to him, the highest judge. Improve when you can. Become better in your own time. I can be patient. I can stay with Regan, I and my hundred knights.

Not altogether so: / I look'd not for you yet, nor am provided / For your fit welcome. Give ear, sir, to my sister; / For those that mingle reason with your passion / Must be content to think you old, and so— / But she knows what she does.

Not quite. I wasn't expecting you yet, and I'm not ready to welcome you properly. Listen to my sister, sir. Those who see your passion with reason must conclude that you are old, and so... But she knows what she's doing.

I dare avouch it, sir: what, fifty followers? / Is it not well? What should you need of more? / Yea, or so many, sith that both charge and danger / Speak 'gainst so great a number? How in one house / Should many people, under two commands, / Hold amity? 'Tis hard; almost impossible.

I dare say it is, sir. What, fifty followers? Isn't that enough? What do you need more for? Or even that many, since both cost and danger argue against so many? How can many people in one house, under two masters, keep the peace? It's hard, almost impossible.
Why might not you, my lord, receive attendance / From those that she calls servants, or from mine?
Why couldn't you, my lord, be looked after by her servants, or by mine?

Why not, my lord? If then they chanc'd to slack you, / We could control them. If you will come to me,— / For now I spy a danger,—I entreat you / To bring but five-and-twenty: to no more / Will I give place or notice.

Why not, my lord? If they happened to neglect you, we could control them. If you come to me, since I now see a danger, I beg you to bring only twenty-five. I won't make room for or recognise any more.
And in good time you gave it.
And it was high time you gave it.
Made you my guardians, my depositaries; / But kept a reservation to be follow'd / With such a number. What, must I come to you / With five-and-twenty, Regan? said you so?
...made you my guardians, the keepers of my wealth, but kept the condition that I'd be followed by a certain number. What, must I come to you with twenty-five, Regan? Is that what you said?
And speak't again my lord; no more with me.
And I say it again, my lord. No more with me.

Those wicked creatures yet do look well-favour'd / When others are more wicked; not being the worst / Stands in some rank of praise.— / [To Goneril.] I'll go with thee: / Thy fifty yet doth double five-and-twenty, / And thou art twice her love.

Wicked creatures still look good when others are even more wicked. Not being the worst deserves some praise. [To Goneril] I'll go with you. Your fifty is still double twenty-five, so your love is twice hers.
Hear, me, my lord: / What need you five-and-twenty, ten, or five, / To follow in a house where twice so many / Have a command to tend you?
Listen to me, my lord. Why do you need twenty-five, ten or five followers, in a house where twice as many have orders to serve you?

O, reason not the need: our basest beggars / Are in the poorest thing superfluous: / Allow not nature more than nature needs, / Man's life is cheap as beast's: thou art a lady; / If only to go warm were gorgeous, / Why, nature needs not what thou gorgeous wear'st / Which scarcely keeps thee warm.—But, for true need,— / You heavens, give me that patience, patience I need! / You see me here, you gods, a poor old man, / As full of grief as age; wretched in both! / If it be you that stirs these daughters' hearts / Against their father, fool me not so much / To bear it tamely; touch me with noble anger, / And let not women's weapons, water-drops, / Stain my man's cheeks!—No, you unnatural hags, / I will have such revenges on you both / That all the world shall,—I will do such things,— / What they are yet, I know not; but they shall be / The terrors of the earth. You think I'll weep; / No, I'll not weep:— / I have full cause of weeping; but this heart / Shall break into a hundred thousand flaws / Or ere I'll weep.—O fool, I shall go mad!

Oh, don't argue about need! Our lowest beggars have something more than they need, even if it's the poorest thing. If you don't allow human nature more than it needs, a man's life is as cheap as an animal's. You are a lady. If being warm were all it took to be gorgeous, nature wouldn't need the gorgeous clothes you wear, which hardly keep you warm. But as for true need... You heavens, give me patience, patience is what I need! You see me here, you gods, a poor old man, as full of grief as of years, wretched in both! If it's you who stir these daughters' hearts against their father, don't make me such a fool as to take it meekly. Fill me with noble anger, and don't let women's weapons, tears, stain my man's cheeks! No, you unnatural witches, I'll have such revenge on you both that the whole world will... I will do such things... What they are I don't know yet, but they'll be the terror of the earth. You think I'll weep. No, I won't weep. I have every reason to weep, but this heart will break into a hundred thousand pieces before I weep. Oh Fool, I'll go mad!
Let us withdraw; 'twill be a storm.
Let's go inside. There's going to be a storm.
This house is little: the old man and his people / Cannot be well bestow'd.
This house is small. The old man and his people can't be properly lodged.
'Tis his own blame; hath put himself from rest / And must needs taste his folly.
It's his own fault. He's shut himself out from comfort and must suffer for his folly.
For his particular, I'll receive him gladly, / But not one follower.
As for him personally, I'll take him in gladly, but not a single follower.
So am I purpos'd. / Where is my lord of Gloster?
That's my intention too. Where is my lord of Gloster?
Followed the old man forth:—he is return'd.
He followed the old man out. He's back.
The king is in high rage.
The King is in a terrible rage.
He calls to horse; but will I know not whither.
He's calling for his horses, but I don't know where he's going.
'Tis best to give him way; he leads himself.
It's best to let him go. He's his own guide.
My lord, entreat him by no means to stay.
My lord, don't beg him to stay on any account.
Alack, the night comes on, and the high winds / Do sorely ruffle; for many miles about / There's scarce a bush.
Oh dear, night is falling, and the high winds are raging. For many miles around there's hardly a bush.

O, sir, to wilful men / The injuries that they themselves procure / Must be their schoolmasters. Shut up your doors: / He is attended with a desperate train; / And what they may incense him to, being apt / To have his ear abus'd, wisdom bids fear.

Oh, sir, stubborn men must be taught by the injuries they bring on themselves. Lock your doors. He has a desperate gang with him, and since he's ready to listen to lies, wisdom tells us to fear what they might stir him up to do.
Shut up your doors, my lord; 'tis a wild night: / My Regan counsels well: come out o' the storm.
Lock your doors, my lord. It's a wild night. My Regan gives good advice. Come in out of the storm.
Who's there, apart from the foul weather?
One minded like the weather, most unquietly.
Someone whose mind is like the weather: very troubled.
I know you. Where's the king?
I know you. Where's the King?

Contending with the fretful elements; / Bids the wind blow the earth into the sea, / Or swell the curled waters 'bove the main, / That things might change or cease; tears his white hair, / Which the impetuous blasts, with eyeless rage, / Catch in their fury and make nothing of; / Strives in his little world of man to outscorn / The to-and-fro-conflicting wind and rain. / This night, wherein the cub-drawn bear would couch, / The lion and the belly-pinched wolf / Keep their fur dry, unbonneted he runs, / And bids what will take all.

Fighting with the furious elements. He orders the wind to blow the land into the sea, or to raise the curling waves above the mainland, so that everything might change or end. He tears his white hair, which the violent gusts, in their blind rage, catch up and toss about like nothing. In his little human world he tries to outdo the wind and rain beating back and forth. On this night, when even the bear with her cubs sucked dry would stay in her den, and the lion and the starving wolf keep their fur dry, he runs about with no hat and dares whatever will to take everything.
None but the fool, who labours to out-jest / His heart-struck injuries.
No one but the Fool, who works hard to joke away the injuries that have broken his heart.

Sir, I do know you; / And dare, upon the warrant of my note, / Commend a dear thing to you. There is division, / Although as yet the face of it be cover'd / With mutual cunning, 'twixt Albany and Cornwall; / Who have,—as who have not, that their great stars / Throne and set high?—servants, who seem no less, / Which are to France the spies and speculations / Intelligent of our state; what hath been seen, / Either in snuffs and packings of the dukes; / Or the hard rein which both of them have borne / Against the old kind king; or something deeper, / Whereof, perchance, these are but furnishings;— / But, true it is, from France there comes a power / Into this scatter'd kingdom; who already, / Wise in our negligence, have secret feet / In some of our best ports, and are at point / To show their open banner.—Now to you: / If on my credit you dare build so far / To make your speed to Dover, you shall find / Some that will thank you making just report / Of how unnatural and bemadding sorrow / The king hath cause to plain. / I am a gentleman of blood and breeding; / And from some knowledge and assurance offer / This office to you.

Sir, I know you, and on the strength of what I've observed of you I dare to trust you with something important. There is a split, though so far both sides are hiding it with cunning, between Albany and Cornwall. Like everyone whose lucky stars have raised them high, they have servants who seem loyal but are really spies for France, sending information about our state: whether about the dukes' quarrels and plots, or the harsh treatment both have given the kind old King, or something deeper, of which these are perhaps just the outward signs. But it's true that an army is coming from France into this divided kingdom. Taking advantage of our carelessness, they have already secretly landed at some of our best ports and are about to show their flag openly. Now, as for you: if you trust me enough to hurry to Dover, you'll find someone who will thank you for giving an accurate report of the unnatural, maddening sorrow the King has reason to complain of. I'm a gentleman of good family and upbringing, and I offer you this task because I know and trust you.
I will talk further with you.
I'll talk to you more about this.

No, do not. / For confirmation that I am much more / Than my out wall, open this purse, and take / What it contains. If you shall see Cordelia,— / As fear not but you shall,—show her this ring; / And she will tell you who your fellow is / That yet you do not know. Fie on this storm! / I will go seek the king.

No, don't. To prove I'm much more than I look on the outside, open this purse and take what's in it. If you see Cordelia, and don't worry, you will, show her this ring, and she'll tell you who your companion is, whom you don't yet know. Curse this storm! I'll go and look for the King.
Give me your hand: have you no more to say?
Give me your hand. Have you nothing more to say?
Few words, but, to effect, more than all yet,— / That, when we have found the king,—in which your pain / That way, I'll this,—he that first lights on him / Holla the other.
Only a few words, but more important than all the rest: when we find the King, and you search that way while I search this, whoever finds him first must shout to the other.

Blow, winds, and crack your cheeks! rage! blow! / You cataracts and hurricanoes, spout / Till you have drench'd our steeples, drown'd the cocks! / You sulphurous and thought-executing fires, / Vaunt couriers to oak-cleaving thunderbolts, / Singe my white head! And thou, all-shaking thunder, / Strike flat the thick rotundity o' the world! / Crack nature's moulds, all germens spill at once, / That make ingrateful man!

Blow, winds, and crack your cheeks! Rage! Blow! You waterspouts and hurricanes, pour down until you have drowned our church spires and the weathercocks on top! You sulphurous lightning, quick as thought, forerunners of the thunderbolts that split oak trees, singe my white head! And you, thunder that shakes everything, strike the round, solid world flat! Crack the moulds nature makes things in, spill all the seeds at once that make ungrateful man!
O nuncle, court holy water in a dry house is better than this / rain water out o' door. Good nuncle, in; and ask thy daughters / blessing: here's a night pities nether wise men nor fools.

Oh uncle, flattering words at court in a dry house are better than this rainwater outdoors. Good uncle, go in, and ask your daughters' blessing. This is a night that pities neither wise men nor fools.

Rumble thy bellyful! Spit, fire! spout, rain! / Nor rain, wind, thunder, fire are my daughters: / I tax not you, you elements, with unkindness; / I never gave you kingdom, call'd you children; / You owe me no subscription: then let fall / Your horrible pleasure; here I stand, your slave, / A poor, infirm, weak, and despis'd old man:— / But yet I call you servile ministers, / That will with two pernicious daughters join / Your high-engender'd battles 'gainst a head / So old and white as this! O! O! 'tis foul!

Rumble all you like! Spit, fire! Pour, rain! Rain, wind, thunder and fire are not my daughters. I don't accuse you elements of unkindness. I never gave you a kingdom or called you my children. You owe me no obedience. So let your horrible will fall on me. Here I stand, your slave, a poor, sick, weak and despised old man. And yet I call you slavish servants, who have joined with two wicked daughters to throw your armies from the heavens against a head as old and white as this! Oh! Oh! It's foul!

He that has a house to put 's head in has a good head-piece. / The codpiece that will house / Before the head has any, / The head and he shall louse: / So beggars marry many. / The man that makes his toe / What he his heart should make / Shall of a corn cry woe, / And turn his sleep to wake. / —for there was never yet fair woman but she made mouths in a / glass.

A man with a house to put his head in has a good helmet. The man who houses his penis before he has a house for his head will end up lousy, both of them; that's how beggars get married. The man who treats his toe as he should treat his heart will cry out with the pain of a corn and lose his sleep. For there was never yet a pretty woman who didn't make faces in a mirror.
No, I will be the pattern of all patience; / I will say nothing.
No, I will be the model of patience. I won't say anything.
Marry, here's grace and a codpiece; that's a wise man and a fool.
Well, here's royalty and a codpiece: that's a wise man and a fool.

Alas, sir, are you here? Things that love night / Love not such nights as these; the wrathful skies / Gallow the very wanderers of the dark, / And make them keep their caves; since I was man, / Such sheets of fire, such bursts of horrid thunder, / Such groans of roaring wind and rain I never / Remember to have heard: man's nature cannot carry / Th' affliction nor the fear.

Oh dear, sir, are you here? Even creatures that love the night don't love nights like this. The angry skies frighten even the animals that roam in the dark and make them stay in their caves. In all my adult life I don't remember ever hearing such sheets of lightning, such bursts of horrible thunder, such groans of roaring wind and rain. Human nature can't bear the suffering or the fear.

Let the great gods, / That keep this dreadful pother o'er our heads, / Find out their enemies now. Tremble, thou wretch, / That hast within thee undivulged crimes / Unwhipp'd of justice: hide thee, thou bloody hand; / Thou perjur'd, and thou simular man of virtue / That art incestuous: caitiff, to pieces shake / That under covert and convenient seeming / Hast practis'd on man's life: close pent-up guilts, / Rive your concealing continents, and cry / These dreadful summoners grace.—I am a man / More sinn'd against than sinning.

Let the great gods who keep up this dreadful uproar over our heads find their enemies now. Tremble, you wretch, who have secret crimes inside you that justice hasn't whipped! Hide, you bloody hand, you liar who breaks his oath, you pretender to virtue who commits incest! Shake to pieces, you villain, who under a secret, convenient disguise have plotted against men's lives! Close-hidden sins, burst out of what hides you, and beg mercy from these terrible officers of justice. I am a man more sinned against than sinning.

Alack, bareheaded! / Gracious my lord, hard by here is a hovel; / Some friendship will it lend you 'gainst the tempest: / Repose you there, whilst I to this hard house,— / More harder than the stones whereof 'tis rais'd; / Which even but now, demanding after you, / Denied me to come in,—return, and force / Their scanted courtesy.

Oh dear, bareheaded! My gracious lord, near here there's a hut. It will give you some shelter from the storm. Rest there while I go back to that hard house, harder than the stones it's built of, which only just now refused to let me in when I asked for you, and force them to show the courtesy they've held back.

My wits begin to turn.— / Come on, my boy. how dost, my boy? art cold? / I am cold myself.—Where is this straw, my fellow? / The art of our necessities is strange, / That can make vile things precious. Come, your hovel.— / Poor fool and knave, I have one part in my heart / That's sorry yet for thee.

My mind is starting to go. Come on, my boy. How are you, my boy? Are you cold? I'm cold myself. Where is this straw, my friend? Need has a strange skill: it can make worthless things precious. Come, to your hut. Poor Fool and boy, there's a part of my heart that still feels sorry for you.
He that has and a little tiny wit— / With hey, ho, the wind and the rain,— / Must make content with his fortunes fit, / For the rain it raineth every day.
He who has only a little tiny brain, with hey, ho, the wind and the rain, must be happy with the fortune that fits it, for the rain it rains every day.
True, boy.—Come, bring us to this hovel.
True, boy. Come, take us to this hut.

This is a brave night to cool a courtezan.— / I'll speak a prophecy ere I go:— / When priests are more in word than matter; / When brewers mar their malt with water; / When nobles are their tailors' tutors; / No heretics burn'd, but wenches' suitors; / When every case in law is right; / No squire in debt nor no poor knight; / When slanders do not live in tongues; / Nor cutpurses come not to throngs; / When usurers tell their gold i' the field; / And bawds and whores do churches build;— / Then shall the realm of Albion / Come to great confusion: / Then comes the time, who lives to see't, / That going shall be us'd with feet. / This prophecy Merlin shall make; for I live before his time.

This is a fine night to cool down a prostitute. I'll make a prophecy before I go. When priests talk more than they practise, when brewers spoil their malt with water, when nobles teach their tailors fashion, when no heretics are burned, only lovers burning with disease; when every law case is fair, no squire is in debt and no knight is poor; when slander doesn't live on people's tongues, and pickpockets don't come into crowds; when moneylenders count their gold in the open, and pimps and whores build churches: then the kingdom of Britain will fall into great confusion. Then the time will come, for anyone who lives to see it, when feet will be used for walking. Merlin will make this prophecy, for I live before his time.

Alack, alack, Edmund, I like not this unnatural dealing. When I / desired their leave that I might pity him, they took from me the / use of mine own house; charged me on pain of perpetual displeasure, / neither to speak of him, entreat for him, nor any way sustain him.

Oh dear, oh dear, Edmund, I don't like this unnatural behaviour. When I asked their permission to help him, they took away the use of my own house and ordered me, on pain of their lasting displeasure, not to speak of him, plead for him or help him in any way.

Go to; say you nothing. There is division betwixt the dukes, / and a worse matter than that: I have received a letter this / night;—'tis dangerous to be spoken;—I have locked the letter in / my closet: these injuries the king now bears will be revenged / home; there's part of a power already footed: we must incline to / the king. I will seek him, and privily relieve him: go you and / maintain talk with the duke, that my charity be not of him / perceived: if he ask for me, I am ill, and gone to bed. If I / die for it, as no less is threatened me, the king my old master / must be relieved. There is some strange thing toward, Edmund; / pray you be careful.

Hush. Don't say anything. There's a split between the dukes, and something worse than that. I received a letter tonight. It's dangerous to speak about. I've locked it in my room. These injuries the King is suffering will be fully avenged. Part of an army has already landed. We must take the King's side. I'll look for him and secretly help him. You go and keep the Duke talking, so he doesn't notice my kindness. If he asks for me, I'm ill and gone to bed. Even if I die for it, as I've been threatened, the King my old master must be helped. Something strange is about to happen, Edmund. Please be careful.

This courtesy, forbid thee, shall the duke / Instantly know; and of that letter too:— / This seems a fair deserving, and must draw me / That which my father loses,—no less than all: / The younger rises when the old doth fall.

The Duke will know at once about this kindness you were forbidden to show, and about that letter too. This looks like a reward worth having, and it should bring me what my father loses: nothing less than everything. The young rise when the old fall.
Here is the place, my lord; good my lord, enter: / The tyranny of the open night's too rough / For nature to endure.
Here's the place, my lord. My good lord, go in. The cruelty of the open night is too rough for human nature to bear.
My good lord, go in here.
I had rather break mine own. Good my lord, enter.
I'd rather break my own. My good lord, go in.

Thou think'st 'tis much that this contentious storm / Invades us to the skin: so 'tis to thee / But where the greater malady is fix'd, / The lesser is scarce felt. Thou'dst shun a bear; / But if thy flight lay toward the raging sea, / Thou'dst meet the bear i' the mouth. When the mind's free, / The body's delicate: the tempest in my mind / Doth from my senses take all feeling else / Save what beats there.—Filial ingratitude! / Is it not as this mouth should tear this hand / For lifting food to't?—But I will punish home:— / No, I will weep no more.—In such a night / To shut me out!—Pour on; I will endure:— / In such a night as this! O Regan, Goneril!— / Your old kind father, whose frank heart gave all,— / O, that way madness lies; let me shun that; / No more of that.

You think it's a big thing that this violent storm soaks us to the skin. So it is to you. But where a greater illness has taken hold, the lesser one is hardly felt. You'd run from a bear, but if your escape led towards the raging sea, you'd turn and face the bear's mouth. When the mind is free of trouble, the body is sensitive. The storm in my mind takes away all feeling from my senses except what beats there. Children's ingratitude! Isn't it as if this mouth should tear this hand for lifting food to it? But I'll punish them fully. No, I won't weep any more. To shut me out on a night like this! Pour on, I'll endure it. On a night like this! Oh Regan, Goneril! Your kind old father, whose generous heart gave you everything... Oh, that way madness lies. Let me avoid that. No more of that.
My good lord, go in here.

Pr'ythee go in thyself; seek thine own ease: / This tempest will not give me leave to ponder / On things would hurt me more.—But I'll go in.— / [To the Fool.] In, boy; go first.—You houseless poverty,— / Nay, get thee in. I'll pray, and then I'll sleep.—

Please, go in yourself. Look after your own comfort. This storm won't give me time to think about things that would hurt me more. But I'll go in. [To the Fool] In, boy, you go first. You homeless poverty... No, go in. I'll pray, and then I'll sleep.

Poor naked wretches, wheresoe'er you are, / That bide the pelting of this pitiless storm, / How shall your houseless heads and unfed sides, / Your loop'd and window'd raggedness, defend you / From seasons such as these? O, I have ta'en / Too little care of this! Take physic, pomp; / Expose thyself to feel what wretches feel, / That thou mayst shake the superflux to them / And show the heavens more just.

Poor naked wretches, wherever you are, who put up with the beating of this pitiless storm, how will your homeless heads and starving bodies, your clothes full of holes, protect you from weather like this? Oh, I have taken too little care of this! Take this medicine, you great and powerful: expose yourselves to feel what wretches feel, so that you may shake off your surplus to them and show that the heavens are more just.
[Within.] Fathom and half, fathom and half! Poor Tom!
[From inside] Nine feet deep, nine feet deep! Poor Tom!
Come not in here, nuncle, here's a spirit. / Help me, help me!
Don't come in here, uncle. There's a ghost. Help me, help me!
Give me your hand. Who's there?
A spirit, a spirit: he says his name's poor Tom.
A ghost, a ghost. He says his name's Poor Tom.
What art thou that dost grumble there i' the straw? / Come forth.
Who are you, grumbling there in the straw? Come out.
Away! the foul fiend follows me!— / Through the sharp hawthorn blows the cold wind.— / Hum! go to thy cold bed, and warm thee.
Get away! The foul devil is following me! The cold wind blows through the sharp hawthorn. Hmm! Go to your cold bed and warm yourself.
Didst thou give all to thy two daughters? / And art thou come to this?
Did you give everything to your two daughters? Is that how you came to this?

Who gives anything to poor Tom? whom the foul fiend hath led / through fire and through flame, through ford and whirlpool, o'er / bog and quagmire; that hath laid knives under his pillow and / halters in his pew, set ratsbane by his porridge; made him proud / of heart, to ride on a bay trotting horse over four-inched / bridges, to course his own shadow for a traitor.—Bless thy five / wits!—Tom's a-cold.—O, do de, do de, do de.—Bless thee from / whirlwinds, star-blasting, and taking! Do poor Tom some charity, / whom the foul fiend vexes:—there could I have him now,—and / there,—and there again, and there.

Who gives anything to Poor Tom? The foul devil has led him through fire and flame, through fords and whirlpools, over bogs and swamps. He has put knives under his pillow and nooses in his church pew, and set rat poison by his porridge, to tempt him to kill himself. He made him proud enough to ride a bay horse over four-inch-wide bridges and chase his own shadow as if it were a traitor. Bless your five senses! Tom's cold. Oh, do de, do de, do de. God protect you from whirlwinds, evil stars and infection! Give Poor Tom some charity, whom the foul devil torments. There, I could catch him now, and there, and there again, and there.
What, have his daughters brought him to this pass?— / Couldst thou save nothing? Didst thou give 'em all?
What, have his daughters brought him to this state? Couldn't you save anything? Did you give them everything?
Nay, he reserv'd a blanket, else we had been all shamed.
No, he kept a blanket, or we'd all have been embarrassed.
Now all the plagues that in the pendulous air / Hang fated o'er men's faults light on thy daughters!
Now may all the plagues that hang in the air, destined to punish men's sins, fall on your daughters!

Death, traitor! nothing could have subdu'd nature / To such a lowness but his unkind daughters.— / Is it the fashion that discarded fathers / Should have thus little mercy on their flesh? / Judicious punishment! 'twas this flesh begot / Those pelican daughters.

Death, traitor! Nothing could have brought a man so low except his unkind daughters. Is it the fashion now that rejected fathers should show so little mercy to their own flesh? A fitting punishment! It was this flesh that fathered those pelican daughters who feed on their parent's blood.
Pillicock sat on Pillicock-hill:— / Halloo, halloo, loo loo!
Pillicock sat on Pillicock Hill. Halloo, halloo, loo, loo!
This cold night will turn us all to fools and madmen.
This cold night will turn us all into fools and madmen.
Take heed o' th' foul fiend: obey thy parents; keep thy word / justly; swear not; commit not with man's sworn spouse; set not / thy sweet heart on proud array. Tom's a-cold.
Beware of the foul devil. Obey your parents, keep your word honestly, don't swear, don't sleep with another man's wife, don't set your heart on fine clothes. Tom's cold.

A serving-man, proud in heart and mind; that curled my hair; / wore gloves in my cap; served the lust of my mistress' heart, and / did the act of darkness with her; swore as many oaths as I spake / words, and broke them in the sweet face of heaven: one that / slept in the contriving of lust, and waked to do it: wine loved / I deeply, dice dearly; and in woman out-paramour'd the Turk; / false of heart, light of ear, bloody of hand; hog in sloth, fox / in stealth, wolf in greediness, dog in madness, lion in prey. / Let not the creaking of shoes nor the rustling of silks betray / thy poor heart to woman: keep thy foot out of brothel, thy hand / out of placket, thy pen from lender's book, and defy the foul / fiend.—Still through the hawthorn blows the cold wind: says / suum, mun, nonny. Dolphin my boy, boy, sessa! let him trot by.

A servant, proud in heart and mind. I curled my hair, wore my mistress's gloves in my cap, satisfied my mistress's lust and did the act of darkness with her. I swore as many oaths as I spoke words and broke them in the sweet face of heaven. I fell asleep plotting lust and woke up to do it. I loved wine deeply and dice dearly, and had more women than the Sultan of Turkey. I was false-hearted, ready to believe gossip, quick to kill; a hog in laziness, a fox in sneakiness, a wolf in greed, a dog in madness, a lion in hunting prey. Don't let the creak of shoes or the rustle of silk dresses betray your poor heart to a woman. Keep your foot out of brothels, your hand out of petticoats, your name out of moneylenders' books, and defy the foul devil. Still the cold wind blows through the hawthorn, saying suum, mun, nonny. Dolphin, my boy, my boy, stop! Let him trot by.

Why, thou wert better in thy grave than to answer with thy / uncovered body this extremity of the skies.—Is man no more than / this? Consider him well. Thou owest the worm no silk, the beast / no hide, the sheep no wool, the cat no perfume.—Ha! here's three / on's are sophisticated! Thou art the thing itself: / unaccommodated man is no more but such a poor, bare, forked / animal as thou art.—Off, off, you lendings!—Come, unbutton / here. / [Tears off his clothes.]

Why, you'd be better in your grave than facing this extreme weather with your body uncovered. Is man no more than this? Look at him closely. You owe the silkworm no silk, the animal no leather, the sheep no wool, the civet cat no perfume. Ha! Three of us here are artificial! You are the real thing. Man without the comforts of civilisation is no more than a poor, bare, two-legged animal like you. Off, off, you borrowed clothes! Come, unbutton here. [He tears off his clothes.]

Pr'ythee, nuncle, be contented; 'tis a naughty night to swim / in.—Now a little fire in a wild field were like an old lecher's / heart,—a small spark, all the rest on's body cold.—Look, here / comes a walking fire.

Please, uncle, calm down. It's a nasty night to swim in. A little fire in a wild field now would be like an old lecher's heart: a small spark, and all the rest of his body cold. Look, here comes a walking fire.

This is the foul fiend Flibbertigibbet: he begins at curfew, / and walks till the first cock; he gives the web and the pin, / squints the eye, and makes the harelip; mildews the white wheat, / and hurts the poor creature of earth. / Swithold footed thrice the old; / He met the nightmare, and her nine-fold; / Bid her alight / And her troth plight, / And aroint thee, witch, aroint thee!

This is the foul devil Flibbertigibbet. He starts at curfew and walks until the first cock crows. He gives people cataracts in the eye, makes them squint, gives them harelips, rots the white wheat with mildew and hurts the poor creatures of the earth. Saint Withold walked over the hill three times. He met the nightmare demon and her nine imps, told her to get off the sleeper and promise to do no harm, and be gone, witch, be gone!
Who's there? What is't you seek?
Who's there? What are you looking for?
What are you there? Your names?
Who are you there? Your names?

Poor Tom; that eats the swimming frog, the toad, the todpole, the / wall-newt and the water; that in the fury of his heart, when the / foul fiend rages, eats cow-dung for sallets; swallows the old rat / and the ditch-dog; drinks the green mantle of the standing pool; / who is whipped from tithing to tithing, and stocked, punished, / and imprisoned; who hath had three suits to his back, six shirts / to his body, horse to ride, and weapons to wear;— / But mice and rats, and such small deer, / Have been Tom's food for seven long year. / Beware my follower.—Peace, Smulkin; peace, thou fiend!

Poor Tom, who eats the swimming frog, the toad, the tadpole, the wall lizard and the water newt. In the fury of his heart, when the foul devil rages, he eats cow dung as salad, swallows old rats and dead dogs from ditches, and drinks the green scum on stagnant ponds. He's whipped from parish to parish, put in the stocks, punished and imprisoned. He used to have three suits for his back, six shirts for his body, a horse to ride and a sword to wear. But mice and rats and such small animals have been Tom's food for seven long years. Beware of the devil who follows me. Quiet, Smulkin! Quiet, you devil!
What, hath your grace no better company?
What, has your grace no better company than this?
The prince of darkness is a gentleman: / Modo he's call'd, and Mahu.
The Prince of Darkness is a gentleman. He's called Modo, and Mahu.
Our flesh and blood, my lord, is grown so vile / That it doth hate what gets it.
Our children, my lord, have become so wicked that they hate the parents who made them.

Go in with me: my duty cannot suffer / To obey in all your daughters' hard commands; / Though their injunction be to bar my doors, / And let this tyrannous night take hold upon you, / Yet have I ventur'd to come seek you out / And bring you where both fire and food is ready.

Come in with me. My duty won't let me obey all your daughters' harsh orders. Though they have ordered me to lock my doors and let this cruel night take hold of you, I have dared to come and find you, and bring you where there is both a fire and food ready.
First let me talk with this philosopher.— / What is the cause of thunder?
First let me talk to this philosopher. What is the cause of thunder?
Good my lord, take his offer; go into the house.
My good lord, accept his offer. Go into the house.
I'll talk a word with this same learned Theban.— / What is your study?
I'll have a word with this same learned scholar. What do you study?
How to prevent the fiend and to kill vermin.
How to keep off the devil and kill vermin.
Let me ask you one word in private.
Let me ask you a word in private.
Importune him once more to go, my lord; / His wits begin to unsettle.
Urge him once more to go, my lord. His mind is starting to go.

Canst thou blame him? / His daughters seek his death:—ah, that good Kent!— / He said it would be thus,—poor banish'd man!— / Thou say'st the king grows mad; I'll tell thee, friend, / I am almost mad myself: I had a son, / Now outlaw'd from my blood; he sought my life / But lately, very late: I lov'd him, friend,— / No father his son dearer: true to tell thee,

Can you blame him? His daughters want him dead. Ah, that good Kent! He said it would be like this, poor banished man! You say the King is going mad. I tell you, friend, I'm almost mad myself. I had a son, now disowned and outlawed. He tried to kill me only recently, very recently. I loved him, friend. No father ever loved his son more. To tell you the truth...
The grief hath craz'd my wits.—What a night's this!— / I do beseech your grace,—
...the grief has driven me out of my mind. What a night this is! I beg your grace...
O, cry you mercy, sir.— / Noble philosopher, your company.
Oh, I beg your pardon, sir. Noble philosopher, keep me company.
In, fellow, there, into the hovel; keep thee warm.
In you go, fellow, there, into the hut. Keep warm.
With him; / I will keep still with my philosopher.
With him. I'll stay with my philosopher.
Good my lord, soothe him; let him take the fellow.
My good lord, humour him. Let him take the fellow.
Sirrah, come on; go along with us.
Come on, fellow, come with us.
Child Rowland to the dark tower came, / His word was still—Fie, foh, and fum, / I smell the blood of a British man.
Young Roland came to the dark tower. His words were always: 'Fie, foh and fum, I smell the blood of a British man.'
I will have my revenge ere I depart his house.
I'll have my revenge before I leave his house.
How, my lord, I may be censured, that nature thus gives way to / loyalty, something fears me to think of.
It frightens me a little, my lord, to think how I may be judged for putting loyalty above a son's natural feeling like this.
I now perceive it was not altogether your brother's evil / disposition made him seek his death; but a provoking merit, set / a-work by a reproveable badness in himself.
I see now that it wasn't only your brother's evil nature that made him want your father dead. It was your father's own guilt that provoked him, stirred up by a wickedness that deserved punishment.

How malicious is my fortune, that I must repent to be just! This / is the letter he spoke of, which approves him an intelligent / party to the advantages of France. O heavens! that this treason / were not—or not I the detector!

How cruel my fate is, that I must regret doing what's right! This is the letter he mentioned, which proves he is a spy helping France. Oh heavens! If only this treason didn't exist, or I weren't the one who discovered it!
Go with me to the duchess.
Come with me to the Duchess.
If the matter of this paper be certain, you have mighty business / in hand.
If what this letter says is true, you have important business on your hands.
True or false, it hath made thee earl of Gloster. Seek out / where thy father is, that he may be ready for our apprehension.
True or false, it has made you Earl of Gloster. Find out where your father is, so he's ready for us to arrest.
[Aside.] If I find him comforting the king, it will stuff his / suspicion more fully.—I will persever in my course of loyalty, / though the conflict be sore between that and my blood.
[Aside] If I find him helping the King, it will make the Duke's suspicion even stronger. [Aloud] I will keep on loyally, even though the struggle between loyalty and my feelings as a son is painful.
I will lay trust upon thee; and thou shalt find a dearer father / in my love.
I'll put my trust in you, and you'll find a more loving father in my love.
Here is better than the open air; take it thankfully. I will / piece out the comfort with what addition I can: I will not be / long from you.
This is better than the open air. Take it gratefully. I'll add whatever comforts I can. I won't be gone long.
All the power of his wits have given way to his impatience:— / the gods reward your kindness!
All the power of his mind has given way to his suffering. May the gods reward your kindness!
Frateretto calls me; and tells me Nero is an angler in the lake / of darkness.—Pray, innocent, and beware the foul fiend.
