Stay till I have read the letter.
Wait until I've read the letter.
I was forbid it. / When time shall serve, let but the herald cry, / And I'll appear again.
I was told not to. When the time is right, just let the herald call, and I'll appear again.
Why, fare thee well: I will o'erlook thy paper.
Well, goodbye. I'll read your paper.
The enemy's in view; draw up your powers. / Here is the guess of their true strength and forces / By diligent discovery;—but your haste / Is now urg'd on you.
The enemy is in sight. Get your army into position. Here's an estimate of their real strength and forces, from careful scouting. But now you must hurry.
We'll be ready when the time comes.

To both these sisters have I sworn my love; / Each jealous of the other, as the stung / Are of the adder. Which of them shall I take? / Both? one? or neither? Neither can be enjoy'd, / If both remain alive: to take the widow / Exasperates, makes mad her sister Goneril; / And hardly shall I carry out my side, / Her husband being alive. Now, then, we'll use / His countenance for the battle; which being done, / Let her who would be rid of him devise / His speedy taking off. As for the mercy / Which he intends to Lear and to Cordelia,— / The battle done, and they within our power, / Shall never see his pardon: for my state / Stands on me to defend, not to debate.

I've sworn my love to both these sisters. Each is suspicious of the other, as people who've been stung are of the snake. Which of them shall I take? Both? One? Neither? Neither can be enjoyed if both are still alive. Taking the widow will enrage and madden her sister Goneril, and I'll hardly be able to win my side of the game while her husband is alive. So for now we'll use his authority for the battle. When that's over, let her who wants to be rid of him think up a way to get rid of him quickly. As for the mercy he intends to show Lear and Cordelia, once the battle is over and they're in our power, they'll never see his pardon. My position depends on me defending it, not debating it.
Here, father, take the shadow of this tree / For your good host; pray that the right may thrive: / If ever I return to you again, / I'll bring you comfort.
Here, father, take the shade of this tree as your good host. Pray that the right side wins. If I ever come back to you, I'll bring you comfort.
Away, old man,—give me thy hand,—away! / King Lear hath lost, he and his daughter ta'en: / Give me thy hand; come on!
Away, old man! Give me your hand. Away! King Lear has lost. He and his daughter are captured. Give me your hand. Come on!
No further, sir; a man may rot even here.
No further, sir. A man can rot here as well as anywhere.
What, in ill thoughts again? Men must endure / Their going hence, even as their coming hither; / Ripeness is all:—come on.
What, gloomy thoughts again? Men must put up with their leaving this world, just as with their coming into it. Being ready is everything. Come on.
Some officers take them away: good guard / Until their greater pleasures first be known / That are to censure them.
Some officers take them away. Guard them well until the wishes of those greater people who will judge them are known.

We are not the first / Who with best meaning have incurr'd the worst. / For thee, oppressed king, am I cast down; / Myself could else out-frown false fortune's frown.— / Shall we not see these daughters and these sisters?

We are not the first who have met the worst while meaning the best. It's for you, oppressed King, that I am cast down. On my own I could outface false fortune's frown. Shall we not see these daughters and these sisters?

No, no, no, no! Come, let's away to prison: / We two alone will sing like birds i' the cage: / When thou dost ask me blessing I'll kneel down / And ask of thee forgiveness: so we'll live, / And pray, and sing, and tell old tales, and laugh / At gilded butterflies, and hear poor rogues / Talk of court news; and we'll talk with them too,— / Who loses and who wins; who's in, who's out;— / And take upon's the mystery of things, / As if we were God's spies: and we'll wear out, / In a wall'd prison, packs and sects of great ones / That ebb and flow by the moon.

No, no, no, no! Come, let's go to prison. We two alone will sing like birds in a cage. When you ask me for a blessing, I'll kneel down and ask you for forgiveness. So we'll live, and pray, and sing, and tell old stories, and laugh at the courtiers in their gilded clothes like butterflies, and hear poor wretches talk about court news. And we'll talk with them too, about who's losing and who's winning, who's in favour and who's out, and take on ourselves the mystery of things, as if we were God's spies. And in a walled prison we'll outlast the gangs and factions of great people, who rise and fall like the tides with the moon.

Upon such sacrifices, my Cordelia, / The gods themselves throw incense. Have I caught thee? / He that parts us shall bring a brand from heaven / And fire us hence like foxes. Wipe thine eyes; / The goodyears shall devour them, flesh and fell, / Ere they shall make us weep: we'll see 'em starve first. / Come.

On sacrifices like these, my Cordelia, the gods themselves throw incense. Have I caught you? Anyone who parts us will have to bring a burning torch from heaven and smoke us out like foxes. Wipe your eyes. The plague will devour them, flesh and skin, before they make us weep. We'll see them starve first. Come.

Come hither, captain; hark. / Take thou this note [giving a paper]; go follow them to prison: / One step I have advanc'd thee; if thou dost / As this instructs thee, thou dost make thy way / To noble fortunes: know thou this,—that men / Are as the time is: to be tender-minded / Does not become a sword:—thy great employment / Will not bear question; either say thou'lt do't, / Or thrive by other means.

Come here, captain. Listen. Take this note [giving him a paper]. Follow them to prison. I've promoted you one step already. If you do what this tells you, you'll make your way to great fortune. Understand this: men must be like the times they live in. Being soft-hearted doesn't suit a soldier. Your important task allows no questions. Either say you'll do it, or find another way to get on.
About it; and write happy when thou hast done. / Mark,—I say, instantly; and carry it so / As I have set it down.
Get on with it, and count yourself lucky when you've done it. Note, I say at once, and do it exactly as I've written it down.
I cannot draw a cart, nor eat dried oats; / If it be man's work, I'll do't.
I can't pull a cart or eat dried oats. If it's a man's work, I'll do it.

Sir, you have show'd to-day your valiant strain, / And fortune led you well: you have the captives / Who were the opposites of this day's strife: / We do require them of you, so to use them / As we shall find their merits and our safety / May equally determine.

Sir, you've shown your brave nature today, and fortune led you well. You have the captives who were our opponents in today's fight. We require you to hand them over, so we can treat them as their deserts and our safety equally decide.

Sir, I thought it fit / To send the old and miserable king / To some retention and appointed guard; / Whose age has charms in it, whose title more, / To pluck the common bosom on his side, / And turn our impress'd lances in our eyes / Which do command them. With him I sent the queen; / My reason all the same; and they are ready / To-morrow, or at further space, to appear / Where you shall hold your session. At this time / We sweat and bleed: the friend hath lost his friend; / And the best quarrels, in the heat, are curs'd / By those that feel their sharpness:— / The question of Cordelia and her father / Requires a fitter place.

Sir, I thought it right to send the old and miserable King to be kept under a chosen guard. His age has a power, and his title even more, to win the hearts of the common people to his side and turn the lances of the soldiers we've conscripted against our own eyes, though we command them. I sent the Queen with him for the same reason. They'll be ready tomorrow, or later, to appear wherever you hold your trial. At this moment we are sweating and bleeding. Friends have lost friends, and even the best causes, in the heat of the moment, are cursed by those who feel their sharpness. The question of Cordelia and her father needs a more suitable place.
Sir, by your patience, / I hold you but a subject of this war, / Not as a brother.
Sir, if you'll excuse me, I regard you only as a subordinate in this war, not as an equal.

That's as we list to grace him. / Methinks our pleasure might have been demanded / Ere you had spoke so far. He led our powers; / Bore the commission of my place and person; / The which immediacy may well stand up / And call itself your brother.

That depends on how we choose to honour him. I think you might have asked what I wanted before you said so much. He led my armies and carried the authority of my rank and person. Being so closely connected with me, he may well stand up and call himself your brother.
Not so hot: / In his own grace he doth exalt himself, / More than in your addition.
Not so fast. He's raised high by his own merit, more than by the titles you give him.
In my rights / By me invested, he compeers the best.
With my rights, which I've given him, he is equal to the best.
That were the most if he should husband you.
That would be most true if he married you.
Jokers often turn out to be prophets.
Holla, holla! / That eye that told you so look'd but asquint.
Hey, hey! The eye that told you that was squinting.

Lady, I am not well; else I should answer / From a full-flowing stomach.—General, / Take thou my soldiers, prisoners, patrimony; / Dispose of them, of me; the walls are thine: / Witness the world that I create thee here / My lord and master.

Lady, I'm not well, or I'd answer you with all my anger. General, take my soldiers, prisoners and inheritance. Do what you like with them, and with me. The fortress of my heart is yours. Let the world witness that I make you my lord and master here.
Do you intend to have him?
The let-alone lies not in your good will.
Stopping it isn't up to you.
[To Edmund.] Let the drum strike, and prove my title thine.
[To Edmund] Let the drum beat and prove that my title is yours.

Stay yet; hear reason.—Edmund, I arrest thee / On capital treason; and, in thine arrest, / This gilded serpent [pointing to Goneril.],—For your claim, fair / sister, / I bar it in the interest of my wife; / 'Tis she is subcontracted to this lord, / And I, her husband, contradict your bans. / If you will marry, make your loves to me,— / My lady is bespoke.

Wait. Listen to reason. Edmund, I arrest you for high treason, and along with you this gilded snake [pointing to Goneril]. As for your claim, fair sister, I block it on behalf of my wife. She's already engaged to this lord, and I, her husband, object to your marriage. If you want to marry, court me. My lady is already spoken for.

Thou art arm'd, Gloster:—let the trumpet sound: / If none appear to prove upon thy person / Thy heinous, manifest, and many treasons, / There is my pledge [throwing down a glove]; I'll prove it on thy / heart, / Ere I taste bread, thou art in nothing less / Than I have here proclaim'd thee.

You are armed, Gloster. Let the trumpet sound. If no one appears to prove your terrible, obvious and many treasons on your body, there's my challenge [throwing down a glove]. I'll prove on your heart, before I eat bread again, that you are everything I've declared you to be.
[Aside.] If not, I'll ne'er trust medicine.
[Aside] If you weren't, I'd never trust poison again.

There's my exchange [throwing down a glove]: what in the world he / is / That names me traitor, villain-like he lies: / Call by thy trumpet: he that dares approach, / On him, on you, who not? I will maintain / My truth and honour firmly.

There's my answer [throwing down a glove]. Whoever in the world calls me a traitor lies like a villain. Call with your trumpet. Whoever dares come forward, him, or you, or anyone, I'll defend my truth and honour firmly.
Trust to thy single virtue; for thy soldiers, / All levied in my name, have in my name / Took their discharge.
Rely on your own courage alone, because your soldiers, all recruited in my name, have been dismissed in my name.
She is not well. Convey her to my tent.
She isn't well. Take her to my tent.
Come hither, herald.—Let the trumpet sound,— / And read out this.
Come here, herald. Let the trumpet sound, and read this out.

[Reads.] 'If any man of quality or degree within the lists of / the army will maintain upon Edmund, supposed Earl of Gloster, / that he is a manifold traitor, let him appear by the third sound / of the trumpet. He is bold in his defence.'

[Reads] 'If any man of rank or position in the army will declare that Edmund, so-called Earl of Gloster, is a traitor many times over, let him appear by the third sound of the trumpet. Edmund is ready to defend himself.'
Ask him his purposes, why he appears / Upon this call o' the trumpet.
Ask him what he wants, and why he appears at this call of the trumpet.
What are you? / Your name, your quality? and why you answer / This present summons?
Who are you? Your name, your rank? And why do you answer this summons?
Know, my name is lost; / By treason's tooth bare-gnawn and canker-bit. / Yet am I noble as the adversary / I come to cope.
Know that my name is lost, gnawed bare and eaten away by the tooth of treason. Yet I'm as noble as the opponent I come to fight.
What's he that speaks for Edmund Earl of Gloster?
Who speaks for Edmund, Earl of Gloster?
He himself. What do you say to him?

Draw thy sword, / That, if my speech offend a noble heart, / Thy arm may do thee justice: here is mine. / Behold, it is the privilege of mine honours, / My oath, and my profession: I protest,— / Maugre thy strength, youth, place, and eminence, / Despite thy victor sword and fire-new fortune, / Thy valour and thy heart,—thou art a traitor; / False to thy gods, thy brother, and thy father; / Conspirant 'gainst this high illustrious prince; / And, from the extremest upward of thy head / To the descent and dust beneath thy foot, / A most toad-spotted traitor. Say thou 'No,' / This sword, this arm, and my best spirits are bent / To prove upon thy heart, whereto I speak, / Thou liest.

Draw your sword, so that if my words offend a noble heart, your arm can win you justice. Here is mine. Look, it is my right as a knight, by my oath and my profession, to declare this: in spite of your strength, youth, position and high rank, in spite of your victorious sword and brand-new fortune, your courage and your spirit, you are a traitor. False to your gods, your brother and your father, a conspirator against this noble and illustrious prince, and from the very top of your head to the dust beneath your feet, a traitor spotted with venom like a toad. If you say 'No', this sword, this arm and all my courage are ready to prove on your heart, which I'm speaking to, that you lie.

In wisdom I should ask thy name; / But since thy outside looks so fair and warlike, / And that thy tongue some say of breeding breathes, / What safe and nicely I might well delay / By rule of knighthood, I disdain and spurn: / Back do I toss those treasons to thy head; / With the hell-hated lie o'erwhelm thy heart; / Which,—for they yet glance by and scarcely bruise,— / This sword of mine shall give them instant way, / Where they shall rest for ever.—Trumpets, speak!

Wisdom says I should ask your name. But since you look so fine and warlike, and your speech shows some sign of good breeding, I scorn and reject the delay I could safely and properly claim under the rules of knighthood. I throw those accusations of treason back at your head, and crush your heart with the hellish lie. Since they only glance off and hardly bruise, this sword of mine will open a way for them straight into your heart, where they'll stay for ever. Trumpets, sound!
This is mere practice, Gloster: / By the law of arms thou wast not bound to answer / An unknown opposite; thou art not vanquish'd, / But cozen'd and beguil'd.
This is just a trick, Gloster. By the laws of combat you weren't obliged to fight an unknown opponent. You haven't been defeated, but cheated and tricked.
Shut your mouth, dame, / Or with this paper shall I stop it:—Hold, sir; / Thou worse than any name, read thine own evil:— / No tearing, lady; I perceive you know it.
Shut your mouth, woman, or I'll stop it with this paper. Wait, sir. You, worse than any name, read about your own evil. Don't tear it, lady. I see you know it.
Say if I do,—the laws are mine, not thine: / Who can arraign me for't?
What if I do? The laws are mine, not yours. Who can put me on trial for it?
Most monstrous! / Know'st thou this paper?
Most monstrous! Do you know this paper?
Ask me not what I know.
Don't ask me what I know.
Go after her: she's desperate; govern her. / [To an Officer, who goes out.]
Go after her. She's desperate. Keep her under control. [To an officer, who leaves.]

What, you have charg'd me with, that have I done; / And more, much more; the time will bring it out: / 'Tis past, and so am I.—But what art thou / That hast this fortune on me? If thou'rt noble, / I do forgive thee.
What you've accused me of, I have done, and more, much more. Time will reveal it. It's in the past, and so am I. But who are you, who have won this fortune over me? If you're noble, I forgive you.

Let's exchange charity. / I am no less in blood than thou art, Edmund; / If more, the more thou hast wrong'd me. / My name is Edgar, and thy father's son. / The gods are just, and of our pleasant vices / Make instruments to plague us: / The dark and vicious place where thee he got / Cost him his eyes.

Let's exchange forgiveness. I'm no lower in birth than you, Edmund. If I'm higher, you've wronged me all the more. My name is Edgar, and I'm your father's son. The gods are just, and they make our pleasant sins into tools to punish us. The dark and sinful place where he conceived you cost him his eyes.
Thou hast spoken right; 'tis true; / The wheel is come full circle; I am here.
You've spoken rightly. It's true. The wheel has come full circle. Here I am, at the bottom.
Methought thy very gait did prophesy / A royal nobleness:—I must embrace thee: / Let sorrow split my heart if ever I / Did hate thee or thy father!
I thought your very walk promised a royal nobility. I must embrace you. Let sorrow split my heart if I ever hated you or your father!
Where have you hid yourself? / How have you known the miseries of your father?
Where have you been hiding? How did you know about your father's sufferings?

By nursing them, my lord.—List a brief tale;— / And when 'tis told, O that my heart would burst!— / The bloody proclamation to escape, / That follow'd me so near,—O, our lives' sweetness! / That with the pain of death we'd hourly die / Rather than die at once!)—taught me to shift / Into a madman's rags; to assume a semblance / That very dogs disdain'd; and in this habit / Met I my father with his bleeding rings, / Their precious stones new lost; became his guide, / Led him, begg'd for him, sav'd him from despair; / Never,—O fault!—reveal'd myself unto him / Until some half hour past, when I was arm'd; / Not sure, though hoping of this good success, / I ask'd his blessing, and from first to last / Told him my pilgrimage: but his flaw'd heart,— / Alack, too weak the conflict to support!— / 'Twixt two extremes of passion, joy and grief, / Burst smilingly.

By looking after him, my lord. Listen to a short story, and when it's told, oh, I wish my heart would burst! To escape the bloody proclamation that hunted me so closely (oh, how sweet life is, that we'd rather suffer the pain of death every hour than die all at once!) I learned to change into a madman's rags and take on an appearance that even dogs despised. In this disguise I met my father with his bleeding eye sockets, which had just lost their precious stones. I became his guide, led him, begged for him, saved him from despair. I never, oh, what a mistake, revealed myself to him until about half an hour ago, when I was armed. Not sure, though hoping, that this would succeed, I asked his blessing, and told him the story of my journey from beginning to end. But his cracked heart, oh dear, too weak to bear the struggle between the two extremes of joy and grief, burst smiling.
This speech of yours hath mov'd me, / And shall perchance do good: but speak you on; / You look as you had something more to say.
This speech of yours has moved me, and may perhaps do some good. But go on. You look as if you have something more to say.
If there be more, more woeful, hold it in; / For I am almost ready to dissolve, / Hearing of this.
If there's more, and sadder, keep it to yourself, because I'm almost ready to melt into tears hearing this.

This would have seem'd a period / To such as love not sorrow; but another, / To amplify too much, would make much more, / And top extremity. / Whilst I was big in clamour, came there a man / Who, having seen me in my worst estate, / Shunn'd my abhorr'd society; but then, finding / Who 'twas that so endur'd, with his strong arms / He fastened on my neck, and bellow'd out / As he'd burst heaven; threw him on my father; / Told the most piteous tale of Lear and him / That ever ear receiv'd: which in recounting / His grief grew puissant, and the strings of life / Began to crack: twice then the trumpets sounded, / And there I left him tranc'd.

This would have seemed the limit to people who don't love sorrow. But one more sorrow, adding too much, would make it much greater and go beyond the extreme. While I was crying out loud in grief, a man came who had seen me at my lowest and avoided my hateful company. But then, finding out who it was who had suffered so much, he threw his strong arms round my neck and roared as if he would burst the sky. He threw himself on my father's body and told the most pitiful story about Lear and himself that anyone ever heard. As he told it, his grief grew overwhelming, and the strings of his heart began to crack. Then the trumpets sounded twice, and there I left him unconscious.
Kent, sir, the banish'd Kent; who in disguise / Follow'd his enemy king and did him service / Improper for a slave.
Kent, sir, the banished Kent, who in disguise followed the King who had made him his enemy, and served him in ways not fit even for a slave.
What does that bloody knife mean?
'Tis hot, it smokes; / It came even from the heart of—O! she's dead!
It's hot, it's steaming. It's just come from the heart of... oh! She's dead!
Your lady, sir, your lady: and her sister / By her is poisoned; she hath confess'd it.
Your lady, sir, your lady. And she has poisoned her sister. She confessed it.
I was contracted to them both: all three / Now marry in an instant.
I was engaged to both of them. Now all three of us will marry in a moment, in death.
Produce their bodies, be they alive or dead:— / This judgement of the heavens, that makes us tremble / Touches us not with pity. [Exit Gentleman.]
Bring out their bodies, whether they're alive or dead. This judgement of the heavens makes us tremble, but it doesn't move us to pity. [The Gentleman leaves.]
O, is this he? / The time will not allow the compliment / That very manners urges.
Oh, is this him? This is no time for the courtesies that good manners demand.
I am come / To bid my king and master aye good night: / Is he not here?
I've come to say good night for ever to my king and master. Isn't he here?
Great thing of us forgot! / Speak, Edmund, where's the king? and where's Cordelia?
A great thing we've forgotten! Speak, Edmund, where's the King? And where's Cordelia?
Do you see this sight, Kent?
Yet Edmund was belov'd. / The one the other poisoned for my sake, / And after slew herself.
Still, Edmund was loved. One poisoned the other for my sake, and then killed herself.
I pant for life:—some good I mean to do, / Despite of mine own nature. Quickly send,— / Be brief in it,—to the castle; for my writ / Is on the life of Lear and on Cordelia:— / Nay, send in time.
I'm gasping for life. I mean to do some good, in spite of my own nature. Quickly send, be quick about it, to the castle, because I've given written orders to kill Lear and Cordelia. Send in time!
To who, my lord?—Who has the office? send / Thy token of reprieve.
To whom, my lord? Who has the order? Send your sign of pardon.
Well thought on: take my sword, / Give it the Captain.
Well thought of. Take my sword. Give it to the captain.
He hath commission from thy wife and me / To hang Cordelia in the prison, and / To lay the blame upon her own despair, / That she fordid herself.
He has orders from your wife and me to hang Cordelia in the prison and blame it on her own despair, saying she killed herself.
The gods defend her!—Bear him hence awhile.
The gods protect her! Carry him away for now.

Howl, howl, howl, howl!—O, you are men of stone. / Had I your tongues and eyes, I'ld use them so / That heaven's vault should crack.—She's gone for ever!— / I know when one is dead, and when one lives; / She's dead as earth.—Lend me a looking glass; / If that her breath will mist or stain the stone, / Why, then she lives.

Howl, howl, howl, howl! Oh, you are men of stone. If I had your tongues and eyes, I'd use them so that the dome of heaven would crack. She's gone for ever! I know when someone is dead and when someone is alive. She's as dead as earth. Lend me a mirror. If her breath mists or clouds the glass, why, then she's alive.
Is this the end of the world we were promised?
Or a picture of that horror?
Let the heavens fall and everything end!
This feather stirs; she lives! If it be so, / It is a chance which does redeem all sorrows / That ever I have felt.
This feather moves. She's alive! If it's true, it's a chance that makes up for all the sorrows I have ever felt.

A plague upon you, murderers, traitors all! / I might have sav'd her; now she's gone for ever!— / Cordelia, Cordelia! stay a little. Ha! / What is't thou say'st?—Her voice was ever soft, / Gentle, and low,—an excellent thing in woman.— / I kill'd the slave that was a-hanging thee.

A plague on you all, murderers, traitors! I might have saved her. Now she's gone for ever! Cordelia, Cordelia! Stay a little. Ha! What are you saying? Her voice was always soft, gentle and low, an excellent thing in a woman. I killed the slave who was hanging you.
It's true, my lords, he did.

Did I not, fellow? / I have seen the day, with my good biting falchion / I would have made them skip: I am old now, / And these same crosses spoil me.—Who are you? / Mine eyes are not o' the best:—I'll tell you straight.
Didn't I, fellow? I've seen the day when with my good sharp sword I'd have made them jump. I'm old now, and these troubles weaken me. Who are you? My eyes aren't the best. I'll tell you in a moment.
If fortune brag of two she lov'd and hated, / One of them we behold.
If fortune boasted of two people she first loved and then hated, we're looking at one of them.
This is a dull sight. Are you not Kent?
My sight is dim. Aren't you Kent?
The same, / Your servant Kent.—Where is your servant Caius?
The same, your servant Kent. Where is your servant Caius?
He's a good fellow, I can tell you that; / He'll strike, and quickly too:—he's dead and rotten.
He's a good fellow, I can tell you that. He'd fight, and quickly too. He's dead and rotten.
No, my good lord; I am the very man,—
No, my good lord. I am the very man...
I'll see about that in a moment.
That from your first of difference and decay / Have follow'd your sad steps.
...who, from the beginning of your change of fortune and decline, has followed your sad steps.
Nor no man else:—All's cheerless, dark, and deadly.— / Your eldest daughters have fordone themselves, / And desperately are dead.
Neither I nor anyone else is. Everything is cheerless, dark and deadly. Your eldest daughters have destroyed themselves and died in despair.
He knows not what he says; and vain is it / That we present us to him.
He doesn't know what he's saying, and it's useless for us to introduce ourselves to him.

That's but a trifle here.— / You lords and noble friends, know our intent. / What comfort to this great decay may come / Shall be applied: for us, we will resign, / During the life of this old majesty, / To him our absolute power:—[to Edgar and Kent] you to your / rights; / With boot, and such addition as your honours / Have more than merited.—All friends shall taste / The wages of their virtue, and all foes / The cup of their deservings.—O, see, see!

That's only a trifle here. You lords and noble friends, know what I intend. Whatever comfort can be given to this great ruined man will be given. As for me, I'll hand back my absolute power to this old king for the rest of his life. [To Edgar and Kent] You will have your rights restored, with extra honours, more than your noble deeds deserve. All friends will taste the rewards of their virtue, and all enemies the cup of what they deserve. Oh, look, look!

And my poor fool is hang'd! No, no, no life! / Why should a dog, a horse, a rat, have life, / And thou no breath at all? Thou'lt come no more, / Never, never, never, never, never!— / Pray you undo this button:—thank you, sir.— / Do you see this? Look on her!—look!—her lips!— / Look there, look there!—

And my poor fool is hanged! No, no, no life! Why should a dog, a horse, a rat have life, and you no breath at all? You'll never come back, never, never, never, never, never! Please undo this button. Thank you, sir. Do you see this? Look at her! Look, her lips! Look there, look there! [He dies.]
He's fainted! My lord, my lord!
Break, heart, I beg you, break!
Vex not his ghost: O, let him pass! he hates him / That would upon the rack of this rough world / Stretch him out longer.
Don't trouble his spirit. Oh, let him go! He'd hate anyone who wanted to stretch him out any longer on the torture rack of this harsh world.
The wonder is, he hath endur'd so long: / He but usurp'd his life.
The wonder is that he lasted so long. He only held on to his life beyond its time.
Bear them from hence.—Our present business / Is general woe.—[To Kent and Edgar.] Friends of my soul, you / twain / Rule in this realm, and the gor'd state sustain.
Carry them away. Our business now is general mourning. [To Kent and Edgar] You two, dearest friends, rule in this kingdom and hold up the wounded state.
I have a journey, sir, shortly to go; / My master calls me,—I must not say no.
I have a journey to go on soon, sir. My master is calling me. I must not say no.
The weight of this sad time we must obey; / Speak what we feel, not what we ought to say. / The oldest have borne most: we that are young / Shall never see so much, nor live so long.
We must bear the weight of this sad time and say what we feel, not what we ought to say. The oldest have suffered most. We who are young will never see so much, or live so long.
